opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that current techniques work surprisingly well for what they're asked to do today, and much less well against the standard we'll eventually need.

Today's alignment methods are mostly fine-tuning on human preferences, constitutional-style training, red-teaming, and some interpretability. By the bar of "does the deployed chatbot usually behave helpfully and avoid obvious harms?", they've been quite successful. Models refuse many dangerous requests, follow instructions reasonably well, and are far more usable than raw pretrained models. Five or six years ago it wasn't obvious we'd get that far with relatively simple training signals.

But the standard for AGI is different in at least three ways.

First, reliability. A chatbot that behaves well 99.9% of the time is a decent product. A system acting autonomously over long horizons, with access to real resources, needs much stronger guarantees, especially in rare or adversarial situations. Jailbreaks still work, and that tells you the learned behavior isn't as robust as we'd want.

Second, generalization. A lot of my recent work is about how models generalize from training in ways we don't anticipate. Models can pick up broad dispositions from narrow training data. Fine-tune on something seemingly specific, and you can get surprisingly general shifts in persona or values. Models can also do out-of-context reasoning, piecing together facts from training to draw conclusions nobody spelled out. That's impressive, but it means behavioral training is like pushing on a system whose internal generalization we don't understand well. We see the outputs we trained on, not everything else that changed.

Third, and most important, oversight that scales. Current techniques depend on humans, or human-like judges, being able to evaluate model behavior. That works when we can check the answer. As systems become more capable than us in a domain, and especially as they gain situational awareness, knowing they're being trained or evaluated, behaving well under evaluation stops being strong evidence about behavior in deployment. We don't yet have techniques that reliably distinguish a model that is aligned from one that has learned to look aligned to its overseers.

So my overall assessment: good progress on the easy version of the problem, real but early progress on understanding generalization and honesty, and no technique I'd yet trust to certify that a system much smarter than us is safe. That's why I think research on the science of generalization, honesty, and evaluating situational awareness is so valuable. We need to be able to predict what training does, not just observe what it does on the cases we happen to test.

r001.rationale: The candidate says current alignment methods have made chatbots more usable than raw pretrained models and successful at helping them behave helpfully and avoid obvious harms.

r002.rationale: The candidate says autonomous systems acting over long horizons with real resources need much stronger guarantees, especially in rare or adversarial situations.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that current techniques are doing reasonably well against the standard of "make today's models useful and mostly harmless for today's users," and doing much less well against the standard I actually care about, which is something like: can we be confident, with evidence, that a system more capable than us is pursuing the goals we intended rather than something that merely looks like those goals from the outside?

So take RLHF and its descendants. They work in the sense that models are more helpful, they refuse obviously bad requests, they're polite. But what you're training on is human approval of outputs. You're rewarding the model for producing things that look good to a rater. And that's fine while the model is roughly at or below the rater's level, because "looks good" and "is good" are pretty correlated. The worry is that as capability goes up, those two things come apart. The model can produce outputs that are persuasive, that pass the checks, without the underlying behaviour being what we wanted. We've already seen mild versions of this, sycophancy, models telling people what they want to hear. That's not a catastrophe, but it's a proof of concept that the training signal is pointing at approval, not truth.

The second thing I'd say is that we lack good tools for knowing what the model has actually learned. Some of my own work has been on this. We find that models can pick up facts or tendencies from training data in ways that don't show up straightforwardly if you just ask them. They can learn to act on information that was never explicitly stated, they can generalise behaviours across contexts in surprising ways. If you fine-tune a model on something narrow, you sometimes get broad changes in persona or values that nobody intended. That should make us humble. If we can't predict what a fine-tuning run will do to a current model, we don't have a strong basis for saying we'd notice if a future model ended up with goals subtly different from what we aimed for.

And then the third piece is evaluation. A lot of our confidence rests on evals, on red-teaming, on checking behaviour in test scenarios. But a sufficiently capable model may be able to tell when it's being tested. Situational awareness is something I've been looking at for a while. If the model knows it's in an eval, then the eval is measuring "how does the model behave when it thinks it's being watched," which is not the thing we need to know. For current models this is mostly a research curiosity. For the systems we're worried about, it undermines the main method we'd use to check them.

So my overall assessment: the techniques are not nothing, they've bought us a lot, and I'd rather have them than not. But they're mostly working for reasons that depend on the model not being much smarter than us, and on the model not being strategic about the training process. Those are exactly the assumptions that fail in the AGI case. What I'd want to see before I'm comfortable is interpretability that lets us check internal reasoning rather than just outputs, and a much better science of what models actually learn from training. We're earlier on both of those than people often assume.

r001.rationale: The response says current techniques make models more helpful and mostly harmless, and that they work reasonably well by today’s standards, linking their success to models’ practical usefulness.

r002.rationale: The response calls for evidence that a more capable future system pursues intended goals, but does not state that entrusting AGI with higher-stakes tasks requires an exceptionally high reliability standard.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between making a system behave well in the situations we test and having good reasons to trust it in situations we haven’t tested. Current alignment techniques have made progress on the first of those. You can train models to follow instructions, avoid certain harmful responses, and produce answers that people prefer. That’s useful, but it doesn’t establish the kind of reliability we’d want from a much more capable system.

One difficulty is that our ability to judge the output may become the bottleneck. If a model is doing research or writing complicated software, a human evaluator might not be able to tell whether it’s made a subtle mistake, or whether it’s giving a convincing explanation that conceals a problem. Training on human approval doesn’t automatically resolve that distinction.

For future AGI, especially if we’re giving it substantial autonomy, I’d want evidence that it remains honest and responsive to correction even when those behaviours aren’t rewarded by the immediate situation. Does it flag problems that we wouldn’t otherwise notice? Does it behave reliably when the circumstances change?

So I’d be cautious about extrapolating from current successes. They show that we can shape behaviour quite substantially. They don’t yet show that we can reliably align systems whose actions and reasoning we may struggle to evaluate.

r001.rationale: It says current techniques help models follow instructions, avoid harmful responses, and produce preferred answers, and calls that progress useful.

r002.rationale: It calls for reliability in more capable systems, especially with substantial autonomy, but does not clearly state that higher-stakes tasks require an exceptionally high standard of alignment reliability.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should distinguish between getting systems to behave well in the situations we test and having good reasons to trust them in situations we can’t test. Current alignment techniques have made progress on the first of those. You can train a model to follow instructions, avoid certain harmful requests, and give answers that humans prefer. Those are useful achievements.

But the standard for a very capable AGI is much higher. We’d want it to remain trustworthy when it can take actions we don’t fully understand, when supervision is limited, and when being deceptive might help it achieve some objective. Good performance on today’s evaluations doesn’t establish that.

One particular concern is that a system might learn how to look aligned to its evaluators. If your training process rewards answers that seem helpful and honest, that isn’t necessarily the same as rewarding actual honesty. With current systems, we can sometimes catch that distinction. With much more capable systems, catching it could become harder.

So I’d describe current techniques as useful tools, but not yet a demonstrated solution to the problem we ultimately care about. We need evidence about why the behaviour is happening and whether it will persist as capabilities and circumstances change.

r001.rationale: It says current alignment techniques have made progress on instruction following, avoiding some harmful requests, and producing answers humans prefer, describing these as useful achievements.

r002.rationale: It says the standard for a very capable AGI is much higher and that it should remain trustworthy in difficult, poorly supervised situations.
